title: SOPs: Cleaning, Guest Communication & Emergency Response

slides.title: Write each routine so a backup can run it from the driveway without calling you
slides.subtitle: Lesson OP.8. SOPs: Cleaning, Guest Communication & Emergency Response
meta: Cedar Ridge: hypothetical lake house, sleeps 8. Owners Maya and Chris live 2 hours away.
Education only. Not legal, fire safety, or insurance advice. In an emergency, call 911.
slides.notes:
After this lesson you'll have a short operating playbook for your house. A backup cleaner or a new co-host can follow it without calling you.

It has three pieces. The first is a turnover checklist. A turnover is the clean between one guest's checkout and the next check-in. The checklist comes with photo proof, supply levels, and a plan for a missed clean. The second is a message sequence, with a named person checking every message. The third is an emergency matrix for seven kinds of incident.

Then we'll run all of it at Cedar Ridge three times. There's a normal Sunday turnover, an internet outage on a Tuesday, and a CO alarm at 1:40 a.m.

Cedar Ridge is the course's hypothetical lake house. It sleeps eight in six beds, and Maya and Chris own it from about two hours away. The people come from OP.7. The cleaner has calendar access. The handyman takes the after-hours calls. Maya owns guest messaging and supplies. Chris handles approvals and bookkeeping, backs Maya up, and makes the owner calls in an emergency. If you haven't built your role map yet, do that first.

slides.title: A usable SOP has seven parts: trigger, owner, steps, standard, proof, escalation, record
rows: What starts it: a checkout, a message, an alarm
One named role from the OP.7 role map
A photo, a timestamp, or a reading
Who to call, by when, if a step fails
Where the result is written down

box.label: One page each
box.text: One page each. If it's longer, split it.

slides.notes:
A standard operating procedure, or SOP, is a written routine that gives the same result no matter who follows it. Most short-term rental checklists fail that test. They say "clean kitchen" and leave the standard to the cleaner's mood that day.

Every SOP in this lesson has these seven parts. The trigger is what starts it. The SOP owner is one named role, taken from your OP.7 role map. One role, not "the team." I say "SOP owner" on purpose, because Maya and Chris own the house, and that's a different thing.

The standard says what done looks like, specifically enough that two people would agree. The proof is a photo, a timestamp, or a reading. Escalation says who to call, and by when, if a step fails. The record says where the result gets written down.

Keep each one to a page. The person using it is standing in a driveway with a phone, often on the day they're covering for someone else.

slides.title: The turnover starts with a walk-through before anything is touched, so damage is on camera
slides.keyline: Trigger: checkout in the calendar. SOP owner: turnover cleaner. Window: 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. (assumption).
rows: Start time recorded in the task app
Damage, missing items, smoke smell, signs of extra guests, items left behind
All 6 beds stripped, used or not
Dishes put away, appliances wiped, fridge emptied, trash out
Toilets, showers, sinks, mirrors, floors; hair check on every surface
Beds made with clean sets from the shelf, same way every time; surfaces dusted, under beds checked
slides.notes:
The turnover runs more than any other SOP. At Cedar Ridge it runs about 61 times a year, once for each base-case stay. Airbnb's ground rules for hosts set cleanliness as an expectation. Hosts should clean between every stay: laundry, trash, vacuuming or sweeping, and wiping surfaces. Your SOP turns that into a standard.

The trigger is the checkout in the calendar. The SOP owner is the turnover cleaner, who has calendar access only, per OP.7. The cleaner logs each step in the task app, the shared app where turnovers are scheduled. The window is six hours, from a 10 a.m. checkout to a 4 p.m. check-in.

Step two is the one I care about most. The cleaner walks the house before touching anything. They note damage, missing items, a smoke smell, signs of extra guests, and anything left behind. Damage gets photographed before cleaning, because after cleaning, the evidence is gone.

Step three strips all six beds, whether they were used or not. That keeps the linen cycle simple and nobody has to guess which beds were slept in.

slides.title: The last six steps check safety and send photos Maya reviews from two hours away
rows: Surfaces, cushions, remotes, floors vacuumed or mopped
Furniture set, grill grates clean, cover on, no guest trash
Alarms in place, status light normal; extinguishers in place; no indoor device; noise monitor and doorbell camera in their disclosed spots; owner closet locked
Each alarm's status light; check logged
Lights off, thermostat to the vacancy setting in the SOP, doors locked
Checklist complete; damage and low stock flagged

box.label: Alarms
box.text: Airbnb says alarms that are present must work and be tested regularly. Each turnover is a visual check of the status light, logged. The button test is monthly.

slides.notes:
Photos serve two purposes. Maya and Chris live about two hours away, so the photos let Maya check the work without driving there. And the photos are evidence if a guest later reports a problem. The retained lesson 9.3 Dealing With Damages covers how to use damage photos in a claim.

Step 10 is the safety check. Airbnb's safety requirements say that if smoke and carbon monoxide alarms are present, hosts must keep them working and test them regularly. So at every turnover, the cleaner looks at each alarm and logs it. The same step checks the noise monitor, the doorbell camera, and the owner closet, which is the owners' locked storage.

The full button test is a separate job. It goes in the monthly inspection, which belongs to the handyman. Set the test schedule using the alarm manufacturer's instructions and your local fire department.

Step 11 sets the thermostat to the vacancy setting you wrote in the SOP. Step 12 is the report. Maya reviews the photos before the guests arrive.

slides.title: Keep four stays of supplies on site and reorder when the shelf drops to two
slides.text: Consumables run about $25 per stay, $1,525 a year across 61 stays. Four stays on hand is about $100 of stock. Par and reorder points are assumptions.
rows: Coffee, tea, sugar, oil, salt, pepper
slides.notes:
Par level means the amount you keep on hand. The reorder point is when someone orders more. Write both on the shelf label. Also write what one stay uses, like how many rolls of toilet paper, so the cleaner can count stays.

At Cedar Ridge, consumables run about $25 per stay. Four stays on site is about $100 worth. Reorder at two. That covers a back-to-back weekend without a supply run.

Linens follow the OP.6 cycle: 18 sheet sets for six beds and 24 towel sets for eight guests. After a turnover, one set per bed is on the bed, one is in the wash, and one is on the shelf. So the shelf should hold six sheet sets and eight towel sets.

For towels, a count of seven is a flag, not an order. A set may still be in the dryer. At six, Maya orders. Sheets have no buffer at this par, so five sheet sets is both a flag and an order.

Anything over $200 needs approval from Maya or Chris first.

slides.title: The missed-clean ladder catches a no-show by 11 a.m., not at 3:30 p.m.
rows: Cleaner confirms in the task app
Maya asks the backup to hold the slot
Call; no answer in 15 minutes, send the backup
Warn the guest; offer a later check-in
Delay check-in, or send a second cleaner
Maya reviews photos; delay check-in if anything is missing
Second miss in 90 days: review whether to keep this cleaner

box.label: What the backup costs
box.text: Same-day premium: $200 instead of $150 (assumption). Four times a year (assumption): 4 × $50 = $200 more. Cheap next to a refund and a one-star review.

slides.notes:
The most visible everyday failure is a guest arriving to a dirty house. Often it starts with a cleaner who doesn't show up and a host who finds out at 3:30 in the afternoon.

The ladder catches it by late morning. The night before, the cleaner confirms in the task app by 8 p.m. If not, Maya calls. If there's still no confirmation by 9, Maya asks the backup cleaner to hold the slot.

On the day, 11 a.m. is the deadline for the arrival photo, not the start time. If it isn't in, Maya calls the cleaner. No answer in 15 minutes, and the backup goes. A backup sent at 11:15 may not finish by 4. So the ladder's real job is to warn the guest early and offer a later check-in.

At 3:45, Maya reviews the final photos. If anything is missing, she messages the guest a delay before 4.

The backup gets a same-day premium, $200 instead of $150. Four times a year, that's $200 more. It's cheap next to a refund.

slides.title: Up to seven messages go to every guest, and Maya checks each one
rows: Thanks, what to expect, house rules, confirm the guest count
Correct guest count and no-party rule
Directions, parking, lake access rules, what to bring
Address, door code, Wi-Fi, house manual
Scheduled; checked in the Monday review
Correct unique code for this stay
Sent by someone who can act
Offer a restock or answer questions
slides.caption: Maya checks every message: each Monday for the week ahead, and the same day for any new short-notice booking.
slides.notes:
Every guest gets the same core messages at the same moments. Automation sends most of them. At Cedar Ridge, Maya checks every one. The mid-stay message only goes to stays of four nights or more.

Airbnb lets hosts send scheduled quick replies automatically. They're triggered by events like a new booking, check-in, or checkout. The same help page says you can skip, send early, or edit an upcoming message without changing the template.

Look at the day-before message. It carries the door code, so Maya checks it in the Monday review and edits or skips it if it's wrong. A wrong code means a family standing on the porch at 4 p.m.

The check-in evening message is manual on purpose. It has to come from someone who can act on the answer.

Every Monday, Maya opens the week's scheduled messages and checks each one against the booking. A booking made midweek for an arrival before next Monday gets the same check the day it comes in.

slides.title: No bot answers a message about smoke, gas, leaks, injury, lockouts, or refunds
items: A person answers any message about smoke, fire, gas, alarms, leaks, injury, police, lockouts, or refunds
A person replies within 30 minutes (assumption), even after an auto-reply
A person checks the lock and sends any code changed after the check-in message
An AI suggestion is a draft until a person approves it, unless it's an approved template
Exceptions (early check-in, late checkout, extra guest) go in the booking notes

box.label: Where this connects
box.text: Tools: SR.5 compares AI messaging tools; OP.4 (Sam's lesson) shows where messages run.

slides.notes:
Automation needs limits. Write these into the SOP and into the settings of any AI messaging tool you use.

The first limit is the important one. No automated or AI reply goes to a message about smoke, fire, gas, alarms, leaks, injury, police, lockouts, or refunds. A person answers those, immediately. Airbnb's scheduled replies fire on events like a booking or checkout. So this limit matters most for AI-suggested replies and any outside tool that answers what a guest writes.

Second, a person replies to any guest message within 30 minutes, even if an automatic acknowledgment went first. The 30 minutes is my assumption.

Third, if a door code changes after the check-in message went out, say after a lockout, a person checks the lock and sends it.

Fourth, an AI suggestion is a draft. A person approves it, unless it's an approved template. Fifth, any exception you grant goes in the booking notes, so the cleaner sees it.

slides.title: The emergency matrix says what to do first, who responds, and who can stop work
rows: Get everyone out, then call 911 from outside
Anyone; Maya or Chris blocks calendar
Everyone out to fresh air, then call 911
911 or fire dept; gas supplier; licensed HVAC
Anyone; closed until fire dept, HVAC, and gas supplier clear it
Shut off water at the main; avoid electrical
Call or message the on-call number (handyman)
Maya resends or resets code; handyman if lock fails
911 for anything serious; first aid kit in manual
Maya or Chris decides if area stays closed
Check the utility's outage page or manual steps
Maya or Chris decides if stay continues
Follow official warnings; shelter in manual
Maya or Chris decides on arrivals
slides.caption: At Cedar Ridge: owner = Maya or Chris; messaging owner = Maya; after-hours contact and on-call number = the handyman.
slides.notes:
An emergency matrix tells the person on the spot what to do first and who to call. It also says who can stop work and what to record. Write it for the guest and the team together. The guest's part goes in the house manual.

On the slide I've filled in Cedar Ridge's people. The written matrix uses roles: owner means Maya or Chris, the messaging owner is Maya, and the after-hours contact is the handyman.

Airbnb's help center says to contact local emergency services first if an emergency is in progress. Airbnb also describes an Urgent Support Line in its app. Neither one replaces 911 or your own on-call person. So the house manual tells guests the order: get out, call 911, then call us.

For fire and CO, the first action has the same shape: get out first, then call. For a leak, the guest needs to know where the water main is, so mark it in the manual.

Every incident gets a record: times, photos, report numbers, and an insurer notice when there's damage or injury.

slides.title: Anyone can stop work for safety, but only an owner reopens the calendar

left.head: Stop-work authority
items: The right to halt a turnover, a repair, or the next booking because something isn't safe
At Cedar Ridge, anyone on the team can use it
Only an owner (Maya or Chris) reopens the calendar
And only after the right professional signs off

right.head: Laminated contact sheet
right.note: Inside the owner closet door, with a copy in the house manual
items: 911, non-emergency police and fire
Utilities and the water shutoff location
On-call phone, handyman, plumber, HVAC company
Insurer's claim line
Fill in real local numbers before the first booking

slides.notes:
Stop-work authority means the right to halt a turnover, a repair, or the next booking because something isn't safe.

At Cedar Ridge, anyone on the team can stop work for safety. The cleaner can. The handyman can. Nobody needs permission to say "this isn't safe, we stop."

Reopening works the other way. Only an owner, Maya or Chris, can reopen the calendar, and only after the right professional signs off. After a CO alarm, the fire department clears the scene first. Then the HVAC technician and the gas supplier clear the house in writing. Stopping is easy on purpose. Restarting is hard on purpose.

The contact sheet is the other half. It's laminated and kept inside the owner closet door, with a copy in the house manual. It lists 911 and the non-emergency police and fire numbers. It lists the utilities and where the water shutoff is. It lists the on-call phone, the handyman, the plumber, the HVAC company, and the insurer's claim line.

Fill in the real local numbers before the first booking. A blank line on that sheet at 2 a.m. costs time.

slides.title: Privacy rules go in the SOPs, because well-meaning people often break them
slides.text: Airbnb bans indoor cameras and recording devices, even if off. Exterior cameras must be disclosed. Noise monitors that don't record are allowed in disclosed common spaces only.
items: Turnover: no new device has appeared indoors
Turnover: the noise monitor is still in its disclosed common-area spot
Turnover: the doorbell camera still points only at the entry
Messaging: camera footage and guest details stay in the platform or the device's own app
Messaging: nobody downloads them to a personal phone or shares them outside the team
slides.notes:
Privacy rules belong in the SOPs, because the people who break them often mean well. A cleaner might want to set up a "nanny cam" to watch for parties. That's not allowed.

Airbnb's device rules prohibit security cameras and recording devices that monitor indoor spaces, even if they're off. Exterior cameras have to be disclosed in the listing. They can't watch indoor spaces or areas like an enclosed outdoor shower. Noise decibel monitors that don't record sound are allowed in common spaces if they're disclosed. They're not allowed in bedrooms, bathrooms, or sleeping areas.

Cedar Ridge has a doorbell camera and a noise monitor, from OP.6. So step 10 of the turnover SOP carries three device checks. The cleaner checks them every turnover, the same way they check the alarms. Two more lines go in the messaging SOP.

Those messaging lines matter because footage and guest details are easy to copy. They stay in the platform or the device's own app.

The retained lesson 9.4 How to Avoid Parties & Smoking covers the party-prevention side.

slides.title: A normal Sunday turnover finishes by 2:20 p.m. and leaves six clean sets on the shelf
slides.text: A family of seven leaves at 10 a.m. after three nights. Eight guests arrive at 4 p.m.

nodes.d: The cleaner confirms in the task app
Walk-through finds a chipped mug and a stained lake towel
Beds stripped, laundry on, then every room and the deck (about 3 hours)
Supplies down to three stays; spares logged; alarms and devices checked
Maya reviews at 2:45. Ready for the 4 p.m. check-in

box.label: The numbers
box.text: Sheets: 18 owned - 6 on the beds - 6 in the wash = 6 clean on the shelf. The $175 cleaning fee covers the $150 cleaner plus about $25 of supplies.

slides.notes:
Now the three walk-throughs. The first is a normal Sunday. A family of seven checks out at 10 a.m. after a three-night stay. The next group of eight arrives at 4. Their door code went out Saturday morning in the check-in message.

The cleaner confirmed at 8:05 the night before. The arrival photo comes in at 10:25. The walk-through finds one chipped mug and a lake towel with a stain.

By 10:40, all six beds are stripped and six used sets go to the wash. When the beds are made, six clean sets come off the shelf. Eighteen minus six minus six leaves six on the shelf, one per bed, so no flag.

Cleaning runs about three hours. At 1:55 the restock drops supplies from four stays to three. The mug comes from the spares shelf and the towel goes to the rag bin. At 2:10 the cleaner does the safety check.

Final photos go up at 2:20. Maya reviews them at 2:45, and the house is ready at 4. The $175 cleaning fee covers the $150 cleaner and about $25 of supplies.

slides.title: When the internet fails, give facts, a credit, and a fix, and leave reviews out of it
slides.text: Tuesday, four-night midweek stay. The listing advertises a dedicated workspace.

nodes.d: No safety words, so an auto-reply is fine. A person replies within 30 minutes.
Maya sends the house manual steps: unplug the router 30 seconds, wait five minutes
Area outage, fix estimated by 6 p.m. No guessing at a restore time
Maya's OP.7 limit (assumption); paid in the platform, not tied to a review
Record times, provider reference, credit, and a root-cause note

box.label: Root cause
box.text: One internet line can't back up an advertised workspace. Chris quotes a cellular backup router. It's over $200, so it waits for the month-end review.

slides.notes:
The second walk-through is a guest problem. On a Tuesday, a guest on a four-night stay messages at 9:05: "Internet is down. I have work calls today." And the listing advertises a dedicated workspace.

The message has no safety words, so an automated acknowledgment is allowed. The SOP still requires a person within 30 minutes. Maya replies at 9:15 with the reset steps from the house manual.

At 9:35 it's still down. Maya checks the provider's outage page. It shows an area outage, with a fix estimated by 6 p.m. At 9:40 she tells the guest what she knows and when she'll update them. She doesn't guess at a time the provider hasn't given.

At 10 she offers a $100 goodwill credit. That's her goodwill limit from OP.7, which is an assumption. She pays it through the platform, not in cash. And she doesn't tie it to a review, because Airbnb's review policy prohibits offering something of value for a review. OP.9 covers that policy and its source.

Service returns at 6:20. Then comes the useful part, the root-cause note.

slides.title: At 1:40 a.m. the CO alarm sounds, and everyone is outside before anyone investigates
rows: "Get everyone outside now, then call 911." Stays on the line until all eight are out
Guest calls 911 (911 should have come first); handyman texts Chris
Handyman drives over (about 35 minutes); doesn't go inside
Fire department finds elevated CO near the propane furnace, shuts off gas
Contacts Airbnb's urgent support line, messages the guest, approves and books a hotel
"Do not occupy" notice on the door; open dates blocked; Sunday's booking flagged
Licensed HVAC inspection; closed until tech and gas supplier clear it in writing
Incident report, report number, findings, receipts; insurer notified
slides.notes:
The third walk-through is a real emergency. It's 1:40 on a Saturday morning. A guest calls the after-hours number because the CO alarm on the lower level is sounding.

The handyman answers. His first words come straight from the matrix: get everyone outside now, then call 911. He stays on the line until all eight guests are out. Notice the order, though. The guest called the handyman before 911, and that cost four minutes. Your house manual should say: get out, call 911, then call us.

The handyman drives over but doesn't go inside. The fire department finds elevated CO near the propane furnace and shuts off the gas.

Relocation costs more than any team member's spending limit. So Chris, as an owner, approves it himself and books a hotel.

At 2:30 it's stop-work. Chris blocks the open dates and flags Sunday's booking for a decision. The house stays closed until the HVAC technician and the gas supplier clear it in writing. Chris notifies the insurer the same day.

box.label: Fix the order
box.text: The guest called the handyman before 911, which cost four minutes. Put the order in the house manual: get out, call 911, then call us.

slides.title: Fill in your emergency matrix with real local numbers, and date each one
slides.caption: Also write one page each for turnover, restock, missed-clean escalation, and messages, using the SOP header: trigger, SOP owner, backup, steps, standard, proof, escalation, record, last reviewed.
slides.notes:
The exercise has two parts. The first is five one-page SOPs: turnover, supply and linen restock, missed-clean escalation, the guest message sequence, and this emergency matrix. Each one gets the same header. Name, trigger, SOP owner, backup, numbered steps, the standard for done, the proof, the escalation, the record, and the date last reviewed.

The second part is on the slide: your own emergency matrix. Don't copy Cedar Ridge's numbers, because they aren't real. Look up the real local ones.

Write the water shutoff location and the shelter location right in their rows. Those are the two things a guest can't find in the dark.

The last column is the date you verified each number. Phone numbers change. Vendors change.

For fire and CO, the first action is already filled in: get out, then call 911. You fill in who responds after that, who has stop-work authority, and what gets recorded. Ask the fire department to look at those two rows with you.

slides.title: Four checks tell you whether your SOPs are finished or still drafts

gates.q: Does every step have a named owner?
Has the backup done the SOP once, for real or in a paid trial?
Does a person send every changed door code and answer every safety message?
gates.no: Change the setting before the next booking

gates.q: Has every SOP been reviewed after the last incident and within six months (assumption)?

slides.end: All four pass: the house runs the same way whoever is on duty.
slides.notes:
These four checks come from the lesson's decision rules. Run them before your first booking, and again after any incident.

First, every step needs a named owner. If a step says "someone checks the alarms," it isn't finished. Put the role there.

Second, a backup has to have done the SOP once, for real or in a paid trial. A name on a list isn't a backup. A person who has already walked your house with the checklist is.

Third, look at your messaging settings. A person should send any door code that changed after the check-in message. A person should answer every message about smoke or a leak. If a tool does either one, change the setting before the next booking.

Fourth, review every SOP after any incident, and at least every six months. The six months is an assumption, so pick your own interval. At Cedar Ridge, the CO incident added a furnace check before heating season. That's what a review is for.

slides.title: The fire department, insurer, and utilities confirm the emergency side of your SOPs
rows: First actions for fire and CO alarms, whether and where this house must have alarms, and how often to test them
Incident notice deadlines, required records, and whether relocation costs are covered
Scheduled messages, safety requirements, and device rules. Check them before you rely on them; these pages change.
slides.notes:
The emergency parts of these SOPs need outside confirmation.

The local fire department confirms the first actions for fire and CO alarms at your house. Ask whether and where your house must have smoke and CO alarms, and how often to test them. What I've shown you follows Airbnb's guidance to call emergency services first. The fire department sets the specifics.

The insurer confirms how fast they need incident notice and what records they want. Ask whether relocation costs are covered. In the Cedar Ridge emergency, Chris booked a hotel at 2:15 in the morning. He should already know whether that's covered before it happens.

The utilities confirm emergency numbers and shutoff procedures. That includes gas or propane, electric, and water. The gas supplier is one of the people who clears the furnace in the example.

And check Airbnb's current pages on scheduled messages, safety requirements, and device rules before you rely on them. These pages change.

slides.next: Next: OP.9 Guest Experience & Review Strategy in the AI Ranking Era. It connects these SOPs to what Airbnb publishes about search and reviews.
slides.notes:
Four actions, each under an hour.

Write the turnover SOP on one page. Use the twelve steps as a starting point, but make the standards fit your house. Add the photo proof column and name the SOP owner.

Go find your water main shutoff. Put a label on it. Add its location to the house manual and the contact sheet.

Fill in the emergency matrix with real local numbers, and write today's date next to each.

Then open your messaging settings. Check that nothing automated sends a changed door code or replies to a safety message.

The house now runs the same way whether Maya, Chris, or a backup is on duty. The next question is how guests experience that work, and what they say about it afterward. OP.9 connects these SOPs to what Airbnb publishes about search. It also shows how to ask for reviews within Airbnb's rules and how to track what guests tell you.

box.label: Cedar Ridge figures
box.text: Cedar Ridge base-case figures used across the course: 61 stays, cleaner $150, cleaning fee $175, supplies $1,525. Par levels, times, and premiums are assumptions.

slides.notes:
Six Airbnb pages back the platform rules in these SOPs. I checked all of them on 2026-09-25 through search summaries.

The ground rules page covers cleaning between every stay and the communication expectations. The safety requirements page covers alarm disclosure, keeping alarms working, and regular testing. The device page covers the indoor camera ban, exterior camera disclosure, and noise monitors.

The scheduled quick replies page covers message triggers, skipping or editing an upcoming message, and AI-suggested replies. The community safety page says to contact local emergency services first. The newsroom post describes the Urgent Support Line in the app.

The Cedar Ridge figures are the base-case numbers used across the course: 61 stays, a $150 cleaner, a $175 cleaning fee, and $1,525 in supplies. The par levels, the times in the walk-throughs, and the backup premium are teaching assumptions.

Nothing here replaces your fire department or your insurer. They confirm the emergency steps for your house.
